paras: The attempted lynching of August Richards took place on 11 November 1888 at Halleck, Elko County, Nevada, when five men with a gallows prepared entered a train car and demanded Richards, who was accused of beating and robbing an elderly local man, from the constable taking him to jail. The constable refused, and the men left without the prisoner. The Elko Independent reported the scene with amusement, and a Winnemucca paper said Richards had narrowly escaped lynching.

Shortly after 10 o'clock on the night of Friday, 9 November, Uncle Billy Hazeltine, a man of about 70 who lived in the Murphy house at Halleck, was attacked at the head of his stairway, beaten, and robbed by someone lying in wait. The Elko Independent first put the loss at $45 and feared he would not recover, adding that if the robber had been caught before leaving Halleck its citizens "would have saved the county the expense of a trial."

On Saturday evening W. J. Hanks arrested August Richards, "supposed to be the man" who committed the robbery, about three miles from Deeth, where he was found in the sagebrush. Richards had served an earlier term in the county jail for malicious mischief and had worked that summer near Peko.

Hanks turned Richards over to Constable McAdams at Deeth, who took him by train toward Elko on the afternoon of Sunday, 11 November. When the train reached Halleck, an "impromptu gallows" with a rope and hangman's noose stood ready, and "a delegation of five determined men" entered the car and demanded the prisoner. According to the Elko Independent, after a few minutes' talk in which the constable said he would guard Richards with his life and kill the first man who laid hands on him, the "would-be lynchers" left the train.

Richards was lodged in the Elko jail, waived examination, and was held to await the Grand Jury. Hazeltine recovered enough to travel to Elko as a witness, and the Independent corrected the amount stolen to $35, noting that $34 was found on Richards. Hanks was to receive the $50 reward and give it to Hazeltine; no report of grand jury action or a trial was found.

Coverage came from Nevada papers, all drawing on the Elko Independent, which ran "The Assassin Arrested" on 12 November and reprinted it in its weekly edition on 18 November. The Independent described the scene as "amusement for the citizens" and dwelt on the prisoner's fear, writing that he was "as white as a corpse, thinking his time had come." Its earlier report on the robbery had already suggested that Halleck residents would have dealt with the culprit themselves.

The Silver State of Winnemucca carried the robbery report on 13 November and on 16 November a condensed account headlined "Narrowly Escapes Lynching." The Eureka Weekly Sentinel reprinted only the robbery report, and the Carson City Morning Appeal noted only the arrest.

The Elko Independent credited the constable's refusal with turning the men away, while the Silver State's condensed version said they consented to leave the prisoner on being told that Hazeltine was likely to recover. The Independent's own full text is the more direct source, since the Silver State was summarizing it.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of August Richards
bases: Five men with a gallows and noose ready entered a train car at Halleck and demanded a prisoner accused of assault and robbery from a constable, who refused, and they left without taking him (A2, A5).

No one was killed: a party of five, acting on an accusation of assault and robbery, demanded the prisoner with a gallows prepared but left him with the constable (A2, A5); this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
Every account of the Halleck confrontation traces to the Elko Independent (A2), reprinted in its weekly (A7, A8) and condensed with credit by the Silver State (A5); no independent report was found.

accounts.label: Elko Independent (full account)
accounts.gist: Five men entered the car beside a prepared gallows and demanded the prisoner; after a few minutes' 'palaver' in which the constable vowed to kill the first man who touched Richards, they left.

accounts.label: Silver State (condensed from the Elko Independent)
accounts.gist: The lynching party demanded the prisoner but, on being told the victim was likely to recover, consented to leave him with the officer.

framing.detail: The Elko Independent had anticipated that Halleck citizens would save 'the expense of a trial' (A1), then described the attempt as 'amusement for the citizens' and mocked the prisoner as 'white as a corpse' (A2).
The Silver State ran 'He Is Captured and Narrowly Escapes Lynching' with a condensed account crediting the Elko Independent.

versions.value: After the constable protested he would guard the prisoner with his life and kill the first man to lay hands on him.
On being informed that the robbery victim was likely to recover.

conflicts.note: Both credit the Elko Independent; A2 is the Independent's own full text and the better evidence. A5's reason may draw on A2's report that Hazeltine was recovering.

record_check.record: accused of said to have beaten and robbed Uncle Billy Hazeltine
record_check.dossier: Richards was 'supposed to be the man who beat and robbed' Hazeltine; an accusation only.
A demand for the prisoner on a train beside a prepared gallows and noose; no siege, seizure or violence reported.
Three papers carried the attempt or arrest (Elko Independent daily and weekly, Silver State, Morning Appeal on the arrest only).

info: The confrontation occurred when Constable McAdams brought Richards by train through Halleck to Elko 'yesterday afternoon' relative to the Monday 12 November issue, i.e. Sunday 11 November 1888.
On the train at the Halleck station.
August Richards, the prisoner; not harmed. His race is not stated.
Uncle Billy Hazeltine, about 70, was knocked down, beaten and robbed at the head of the stairway of the Murphy house at Halleck on Friday night about 10 o'clock.
Unnamed men of Halleck, described as 'a delegation of five determined men' and 'would-be lynchers'.
The men left the train without the prisoner, who was lodged in the Elko jail, waived examination and was held for the Grand Jury.
